summary: Responds to RFC 603 on network connectivity. The author argues that what matters in judging a node with four links is how well the network stays connected after the node fails, not how many circuits are affected, and addresses the points raised there.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone asked if the map of connections was good. This note says the right test is whether the network stays connected when one spot breaks.

subtitle: A reply arguing that what matters is how well the ARPANET stays connected after a node fails.

tldr.problem: RFC 603 questioned whether it was good or bad for a node such as AMES to have four connections.
tldr.mechanism: The author says to judge a node failure by how well the network stays connected, and that the real weak spots are the one-connected and two-connected nodes.
tldr.outcome: He adds that loops are only a means to more connectivity, that circuits cost ARPA money, and that BBN's late December 1973 proposals aimed to break up long chains of IMPs.

sections.title: Responding to RFC 603
sections.content: Alex McKenzie of BBN-NET calls network topology a complicated political and economic question with obvious technical overtones. He does not try to cover every argument, only to respond directly to the points in RFC 603.
sections.plainLanguage: He is only answering some specific points, not writing a whole report.

sections.title: How Connected Is Connected Enough
sections.content:
His first point is that the test of a four-connected node such as AMES is not how many circuits a node failure affects, but how well the network stays connected afterward. If all nodes were four-connected, nobody would call that bad for reliability.

The weaknesses are the one-connected nodes (Hawaii, London) and the two-connected nodes. He agrees that two adjacent three-connected nodes beat a four-connected node next to a two-connected one, but real installations of interfaces and common carrier services make the network grow in sub-optimal ways.
sections.plainLanguage: A town with only one road in is the risky one. A town with four roads is fine.

sections.title: Loops, Cost and BBN's Suggestions
sections.content:
Loops are not good in themselves; they look good because they increase connectivity and reduce the effect of multiple failures. More circuits cost ARPA money, both for IMP interfaces and recurring circuit charges.

BBN had suggested several times that connectivity should be increased, but only in late December 1973 gave specific locations for added circuits. These aimed at breaking the long chains of IMPs that came with growth, and ARPA and NAC were presumably evaluating them.
sections.plainLanguage: New roads cost money. They suggested where to build a few so there would be no very long single-file lines of towns.

references.text: RFC 603, the document being responded to.
